questions.stem: Which helicopter control changes the pitch of all main-rotor blades at the same time to make the aircraft climb or descend?
options: The collective
The cyclic
The anti-torque pedals
The throttle
questions.explain: The collective raises or lowers the pitch of every main-rotor blade together, changing total lift so the helicopter climbs or descends. The cyclic tilts the rotor disc; the pedals control yaw.

questions.stem: The cyclic stick primarily controls the helicopter's
options: direction of horizontal movement
total lift for climbing
engine and rotor RPM
yaw around the vertical axis
questions.explain: The cyclic tilts the main-rotor disc, moving the helicopter forward, back or sideways. The collective sets total lift and the pedals control yaw.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the anti-torque pedals?
options: Control yaw and counter main-rotor torque
Change the pitch of the main-rotor blades
Increase the engine and main-rotor RPM
Tilt the main-rotor disc in the direction of travel
questions.explain: The pedals vary tail-rotor thrust, which counters the torque of the main rotor and points the nose left or right (yaw).

questions.stem: The tail rotor on a conventional single-rotor helicopter exists mainly to
options: counteract the torque produced by the main rotor
generate most of the aircraft's lift in a hover
slow the aircraft down in fast forward flight
provide the aircraft's main forward thrust
questions.explain: By Newton's third law the fuselage tends to spin opposite the main rotor. The tail rotor produces sideways thrust to counter that torque and control heading.

questions.stem: The four forces acting on an aircraft in flight are
options: lift, weight, thrust and drag
lift, torque, thrust and friction
gravity, pressure, lift and yaw
thrust, torque, drag and camber
questions.explain: Lift opposes weight, and thrust opposes drag. In steady flight they are in balance.

questions.stem: Autorotation allows a helicopter to land safely when
options: engine power is lost, letting airflow spin the rotor
the tail rotor fails while hovering in ground effect
the hydraulic boost fails during fast forward flight
the aircraft exceeds its never-exceed airspeed, VNE
questions.explain: In autorotation the engine is disengaged and air flowing up through the descending rotor keeps the blades spinning, storing energy for a controlled flare and landing.

questions.stem: Retreating blade stall sets the practical limit on a helicopter's
options: maximum forward airspeed
maximum hover altitude
minimum turning radius
fuel efficiency
questions.explain: As forward speed rises, the retreating blade sees slower relative airflow and a higher angle of attack until it stalls — capping how fast the helicopter can fly.

questions.stem: Dissymmetry of lift in forward flight refers to the difference in lift between
options: the advancing and retreating blades
the main rotor and the tail rotor system
the root and the tip of a single blade
climbing flight and descending flight
questions.explain: The advancing blade meets faster airflow than the retreating blade, so it makes more lift. Blade flapping equalises this and keeps the aircraft from rolling.

questions.stem: Ground effect improves a helicopter's lift efficiency when it is
options: within one rotor diameter of the ground
at altitudes above one thousand feet AGL
flying at or above its never-exceed speed
descending in a full autorotation
questions.explain: Close to the ground the rotor downwash forms a cushion that reduces induced drag and tip vortices, so less power is needed to hover.

questions.stem: Effective translational lift occurs as a helicopter
options: gains forward airspeed into undisturbed air
descends vertically at a high rate of descent
begins to lose its tail-rotor authority
settles with power into its own downwash
questions.explain: Around 16–24 knots the rotor outruns its recirculating downwash and works in undisturbed air, producing a noticeable gain in lift for the same power.

questions.stem: The swashplate assembly on a helicopter
options: passes cyclic and collective inputs to the blades
generates the aircraft's main electrical power
drives the tail-rotor drive shaft and gearbox
measures and displays the main-rotor RPM
questions.explain: The non-rotating and rotating halves of the swashplate convert the pilot's stationary control inputs into pitch changes on the rotating blades.

questions.stem: Because of gyroscopic precession, a force applied to a spinning rotor disc takes effect
options: about 90 degrees later around the disc
at the exact point where it is applied
180 degrees opposite the point of application
only at the root of the rotor blade
questions.explain: A rotor acts like a gyroscope: an input shows up roughly 90° further around the disc, which is why controls are rigged ahead of the desired reaction.

questions.stem: The U.S. Army's primary attack helicopter is the
options: AH-64 Apache
UH-60 Black Hawk
CH-47 Chinook
UH-72 Lakota
questions.explain: The AH-64 Apache is the Army's dedicated attack helicopter. The Black Hawk is utility, the Chinook is heavy lift, and the Lakota is light utility.

questions.stem: The UH-60 Black Hawk is used primarily as a
options: utility and troop-transport helicopter
heavy-lift cargo transport helicopter
close-support attack helicopter
basic rotary-wing trainer
questions.explain: The UH-60 Black Hawk is the Army's workhorse utility helicopter, moving troops and equipment.

questions.stem: The CH-47 Chinook is unusual among Army helicopters because it has
options: tandem counter-rotating rotors and no tail rotor
no main rotor, only a large tail rotor
four small lifting rotors on outriggers
a single coaxial main rotor and a pusher propeller
questions.explain: The Chinook's two tandem rotors turn in opposite directions, cancelling each other's torque, so it needs no anti-torque tail rotor.

questions.stem: On a fixed-wing aircraft, the ailerons control
options: roll about the longitudinal axis
pitch about the lateral axis
yaw about the vertical axis
thrust from the engine
questions.explain: Ailerons on the wings move opposite each other to roll the aircraft. Elevators control pitch and the rudder controls yaw.

questions.stem: The elevator on a fixed-wing aircraft controls
options: pitch — the nose up and down
roll the aircraft left and right
yaw the nose left and right
the position of the flaps
questions.explain: The elevator on the horizontal stabiliser raises or lowers the nose, controlling pitch about the lateral axis.

questions.stem: The angle of attack of an airfoil is the angle between the
options: chord line and the relative wind
wing chord and the horizon line
fuselage and the runway surface
rotor blade and the rotor mast
questions.explain: Angle of attack is measured between the chord line and the oncoming relative wind. Increasing it raises lift — up to the stalling angle.

questions.stem: An aerodynamic stall occurs when
options: the angle of attack exceeds the critical angle
the engine suddenly stops running in flight
the aircraft exceeds the local speed of sound
the aircraft completely runs out of fuel
questions.explain: A stall is an aerodynamic event: past the critical angle of attack the airflow separates and lift drops sharply — it has nothing to do with the engine 'stalling'.

questions.stem: High density altitude (hot, high and humid conditions) affects a helicopter by
options: reducing engine and rotor performance
noticeably increasing available lift
improving overall fuel economy
having no real effect on performance
questions.explain: Thin air at high density altitude means less lift from the rotor and less power from the engine, so performance falls — a key planning factor in hot, high environments.

questions.stem: Coning of the main-rotor blades is caused by the balance between
options: upward lift and outward centrifugal force
rotor torque and aerodynamic drag
gravity acting against engine thrust
the cyclic and collective control inputs
questions.explain: In flight the blades bend upward into a shallow cone where the upward lift force and the outward centrifugal force reach equilibrium.

questions.stem: Translating tendency (tail-rotor drift) makes a hovering helicopter tend to drift
options: in the direction of tail-rotor thrust
straight up into a vertical climb
nose-down toward the ground
rearward, tail-first, into wind
questions.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust pushes the whole aircraft in that direction at a hover; pilots correct with a slight cyclic input or built-in rigging.

questions.stem: An altimeter measures an aircraft's
options: altitude, using air pressure
indicated airspeed in knots
magnetic compass heading
rate of turn and slip
questions.explain: The altimeter reads static air pressure, which falls with height, and displays altitude. Airspeed, heading and turn rate come from other instruments.

questions.stem: The abbreviation VNE on an airspeed indicator means
options: velocity never exceed
variable normal endurance
vertical net elevation
very near empty
questions.explain: VNE is the never-exceed speed — the maximum airspeed at which the aircraft may be flown, marked with a red line on the airspeed indicator.

questions.stem: A helicopter is most likely to enter vortex ring state (settling with power) when it is:
options: In fast forward cruise flight
Climbing at full engine power
Descending slowly under power
Hovering low in ground effect
questions.explain: Vortex ring state develops in a near-vertical descent above about 300 fpm at low airspeed with power applied, as the rotor settles into its own recirculating downwash.

questions.stem: The correct recovery from vortex ring state is to:
options: Gain airspeed and lower collective
Raise collective to add more power
Enter a steeper vertical descent
Hold the hover and wait it out
questions.explain: Recovery means flying out of the descending air by gaining forward airspeed and reducing collective; adding power only feeds the vortex and worsens the descent.

questions.stem: Dynamic rollover occurs when a helicopter pivots about:
options: Its main rotor mast axis
The center of gravity point
The tail rotor gearbox
A skid or wheel in contact
questions.explain: Dynamic rollover is a lateral pivot about a skid or wheel still touching the ground; once the critical rollover angle is passed, thrust drives the roll and cyclic cannot stop it.

questions.stem: If a helicopter exceeds its critical rollover angle, the pilot should expect that:
options: Cyclic input will right the aircraft
Lateral cyclic cannot stop the roll
Adding collective ends the rollover
The rotor will realign the fuselage
questions.explain: Past the critical rollover angle, rotor thrust continues the roll and cyclic authority is insufficient; the correct action is to smoothly reduce collective before the angle is reached.

questions.stem: Loss of tail-rotor effectiveness (LTE) is most associated with:
options: High-speed forward cruise flight
Steep autorotation descents only
Low airspeed with certain winds
Maximum-power vertical climbs
questions.explain: LTE occurs at low airspeeds, typically below effective translational lift, where wind from certain relative directions overcomes tail-rotor thrust and produces an uncommanded yaw.

questions.stem: Retreating blade stall sets the limit on a helicopter's:
options: Maximum forward airspeed
Minimum hover ceiling
Autorotation glide ratio
Ground-effect cushion
questions.explain: At high forward speed the retreating blade meets low relative airflow and must use a high angle of attack, so it stalls first, capping the never-exceed forward speed (Vne).

questions.stem: Effective translational lift (ETL) is typically felt at about:
options: 1 to 5 knots airspeed
45 to 55 knots airspeed
70 to 80 knots airspeed
16 to 24 knots airspeed
questions.explain: Near 16 to 24 knots the rotor moves into relatively undisturbed air, cutting induced flow and giving a marked gain in lifting efficiency for the same power.

questions.stem: The transverse flow effect during forward flight produces:
options: A steady loss of engine power
Vibration and a rolling tendency
Reduced lift across whole disk
A nose-down pitch at high speed
questions.explain: Uneven induced flow front-to-rear of the disk raises the angle of attack at the rear; through gyroscopic precession this shows up near ETL as increased vibration and a rolling tendency.

questions.stem: Because of the Coriolis effect, a rotor blade tends to:
options: Speed up as it moves inboard
Slow down as it flaps upward
Stall as it moves outboard
Twist toward its leading edge
questions.explain: By conservation of angular momentum, a blade's mass shifting closer to the mast (as it flaps up) accelerates its rotational speed, and it slows again as the mass moves outboard.

questions.stem: Tail-rotor drift (translating tendency) makes a hovering helicopter tend to:
options: Yaw slowly toward the nose
Pitch up about the mast
Drift sideways in a hover
Climb without collective
questions.explain: The tail rotor's sideward thrust pushes the whole aircraft laterally in a hover; designers and pilots counter this translating tendency with cyclic offset or mast rigging.

questions.stem: The drag that results directly from the production of rotor lift is:
options: Parasite drag
Profile drag
Form drag
Induced drag
questions.explain: Induced drag is the by-product of generating lift; parasite drag comes from the fuselage and non-lifting parts, and profile drag from the blade airfoils moving through the air.

questions.stem: Ground effect noticeably improves rotor lift when the helicopter is within about:
options: One rotor diameter of ground
Ten rotor diameters overhead
Fifty feet of an obstacle
Half a mile of a runway
questions.explain: Within roughly one rotor diameter of the surface the ground restricts induced flow and tip vortices, lowering induced drag and boosting lift for a given power setting.

questions.stem: During an autorotation the main rotor is kept turning by:
options: The engine at flight idle
An electric backup motor
Air flowing up through rotor
Fuel stored in the hub
questions.explain: With the engine disengaged, upward airflow through the descending rotor drives it, and the pilot later trades that stored rotor energy in a flare to cushion the landing.

questions.stem: Pendular action describes the helicopter fuselage:
options: Yawing under tail thrust
Swinging below the rotor
Twisting the tail boom
Rolling from ground effect
questions.explain: The fuselage hangs like a pendulum beneath the rotor disk and can overswing when the pilot over-controls; smooth, measured cyclic inputs keep it damped.

questions.stem: Because of gyroscopic precession, a force applied to the spinning rotor takes effect:
options: At the same instant applied
On the opposite mast side
Only near the blade roots
About 90 degrees later
questions.explain: A rotor behaves like a gyroscope, so an input's maximum reaction appears roughly 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation, which is why control rigging is offset.

questions.stem: In a coordinated helicopter turn the anti-torque pedals are used to:
options: Keep the ball centered
Steepen the bank angle
Add main-rotor pitch
Lower the nose down
questions.explain: A slip (ball toward the turn) or skid (ball away) shows an uncoordinated turn; coordinated pedal, with cyclic and collective, keeps the trim ball centered.

questions.stem: A center-of-gravity loaded too far forward tends to leave the pilot with:
options: Extra aft cyclic margin
A nose-high hover attitude
Reduced tail-rotor thrust
Limited aft cyclic travel
questions.explain: A forward CG needs aft cyclic to hold level flight, using up aft control range; an aft CG does the opposite, and both extremes shrink the available control margins.

questions.stem: Shaded areas of the height-velocity diagram (dead man's curve) mark conditions where:
options: Fuel flow is lowest
Autorotation is unsafe
The rotor overspeeds
Cruise is efficient
questions.explain: The shaded low-altitude, low-speed zones are combinations where an engine failure would not leave enough height and energy to complete a safe autorotation.

questions.stem: Which U.S. Army helicopter is the dedicated attack aircraft?
options: UH-60 Black Hawk
CH-47 Chinook
AH-64 Apache
UH-72 Lakota
questions.explain: The AH-64 Apache is the Army's attack helicopter; the UH-60 is a utility aircraft, the CH-47 is heavy-lift, and the UH-72 Lakota is a light utility type.

questions.stem: The tandem-rotor heavy-lift helicopter in U.S. Army service is the:
options: UH-60 Black Hawk
CH-47 Chinook
AH-64 Apache
UH-72 Lakota
questions.explain: The CH-47 Chinook uses two counter-rotating tandem rotors for heavy-lift transport; because the rotors cancel each other's torque, it needs no anti-torque tail rotor.

questions.stem: In forward flight the advancing blade flaps upward. What does this flapping do to the advancing blade's angle of attack?
options: It increases, adding to that blade's lift
It stays fixed unless collective moves
It reverses, so the blade makes no lift
It decreases, reducing that blade's lift
questions.explain: As the advancing blade flaps up, its upward motion changes the relative wind so its angle of attack falls and its lift drops. The retreating blade flaps down and gains angle of attack. Flapping, together with cyclic feathering, evens out lift across the disc (dissymmetry of lift).

questions.stem: In a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above, the onset of retreating blade stall typically shows as low-frequency vibration plus:
options: A nose pitch-down and a roll to the right
A nose pitch-up and a roll to the right
A nose pitch-down and a roll to the left
A nose pitch-up and a roll to the left
questions.explain: With a counterclockwise rotor the retreating blade is on the left. Its loss of lift takes effect about 90 degrees later in rotation, over the tail, so the nose pitches up, and the helicopter rolls toward the retreating (left) side.

questions.stem: A pilot feels the onset of retreating blade stall in high-speed cruise. Which action should come first?
options: Raise the collective to hold the altitude
Lower the collective to reduce blade pitch
Apply forward cyclic to lower the nose
Reduce rotor RPM below the normal range
questions.explain: Lowering collective reduces the retreating blade's angle of attack and is the first step. The pilot then reduces airspeed, eases the maneuver and keeps rotor RPM at the upper normal range. Forward cyclic adds airspeed and deepens the stall; low RPM makes it worse.

questions.stem: Which approach is most likely to lead a helicopter into settling with power (vortex ring state)?
options: A shallow approach into a steady headwind
A steep downwind approach with airspeed near zero
A normal approach holding 60 knots to short final
A running landing at a speed above ETL
questions.explain: Settling with power needs a near-vertical descent of more than about 300 fpm, airspeed below ETL and power applied. A steep approach with a tailwind lets airspeed bleed to near zero while descending, the classic entry. The other profiles keep the rotor moving into clean air.

questions.stem: A pilot misses a tie-down strap still attached to one skid. As the collective is raised for takeoff, the main danger is:
options: Ground resonance from rotor imbalance
Settling with power in its own downwash
Retreating blade stall at liftoff speed
Dynamic rollover about the secured skid
questions.explain: A skid held to the ground becomes a pivot point. As rotor thrust builds, the helicopter rolls about it and can pass the critical rollover angle. Ground resonance comes from blades moving out of phase, not from a fixed pivot.

questions.stem: Ground resonance is most closely associated with which combination?
options: An articulated rotor and a hard touchdown
A semirigid rotor and a low-G pushover
A rigid rotor and a high-speed descent
A tandem rotor and a steep tailwind turn
questions.explain: Ground resonance mainly affects fully articulated rotors. A hard or one-skid touchdown can knock the blades out of phase in their lead-lag motion, unbalancing the rotor so it oscillates in step with the landing gear. A low-G pushover with a semirigid rotor causes mast bumping instead.

questions.stem: Ground resonance begins on touchdown while rotor RPM is still in the normal operating range. The recommended action is to:
options: Hold the aircraft down with forward cyclic
Lift off to a hover to break ground contact
Close the throttle and apply the rotor brake
Lower the collective fully and hold position
questions.explain: With RPM in the normal range, lifting off to a hover removes the ground contact that feeds the oscillation, letting the blades realign. Closing the throttle and lowering the collective is the choice only when RPM is too low to fly.

questions.stem: Mast bumping is a hazard chiefly in helicopters with which type of main rotor?
options: Semirigid two-blade teetering rotor
Fully articulated multi-blade rotor
Rigid hingeless rotor head
Tandem counter-rotating rotors
questions.explain: A semirigid rotor teeters as a unit on the mast. In low-G or abrupt control inputs the hub can exceed its flapping limit and strike the mast, which can sever it. Articulated and rigid rotors do not teeter about a single hinge.

questions.stem: A two-blade teetering-rotor helicopter enters a low-G condition and starts to roll right. The first corrective input should be:
options: Gentle aft cyclic to reload the rotor
Left lateral cyclic to stop the roll
Forward cyclic to steepen the descent
Full up collective to restore thrust
questions.explain: In low G the rotor has little thrust, so lateral cyclic cannot roll the fuselage and may cause mast bumping. Gentle aft cyclic restores positive G and rotor thrust first; only then is lateral cyclic used to level the aircraft.

questions.stem: Rotor RPM decays well below its lower limit while the pilot keeps the collective high. The most direct result is:
options: Mast bumping as the hub teeters
Excessive coning and blade stall
Rotor overspeed in the descent
Ground resonance in the hover
questions.explain: Lower RPM reduces centrifugal force while lift is still being demanded, so the blades cone upward and their high angle of attack leads to stall. Recovery means lowering collective and restoring RPM.

questions.stem: In a steady autorotative descent, rotor RPM is climbing toward its upper limit. To hold it within limits the pilot should:
options: Raise the collective slightly
Lower the collective fully down
Roll the throttle on to full open
Apply aft cyclic to slow down
questions.explain: Raising collective increases blade pitch and drag, slowing the rotor. Lowering collective or applying aft cyclic both increase rotor RPM. The freewheeling unit has disconnected the engine, so the throttle does not control rotor RPM in autorotation.

questions.stem: In a steady vertical autorotation, which part of each blade produces the force that keeps the rotor turning?
options: The outer tip, or driven region
The inner root, or stall region
The middle span, or driving region
The whole span in equal amounts
questions.explain: The driving (autorotative) region, roughly 25 to 70 percent of the radius, has its total aerodynamic force tilted ahead of the rotor axis and speeds the rotor up. The outer driven region creates drag that slows it, and the inner stall region works above its critical angle.

questions.stem: With the engine failed and the helicopter in autorotation, the tail rotor:
options: Stops, because only the engine can drive it
Windmills freely, giving no yaw control
Keeps turning, driven by the main transmission
Locks in place to act as a fixed vertical fin
questions.explain: The freewheeling unit disconnects only the engine. The tail rotor stays geared to the main rotor through the transmission, so it keeps turning and the pedals still give yaw control.

questions.stem: The engine fails in cruise in a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above. The nose tends to yaw:
options: Left, so the pilot adds right pedal
Right, so the pilot adds left pedal
Right, so the pilot adds right pedal
Left, so the pilot adds left pedal
questions.explain: Under power, main-rotor torque pushes the nose right and left pedal holds heading. When the engine quits, torque disappears but the left-pedal tail-rotor thrust remains, so the nose swings left. Right pedal keeps the aircraft in trim.

questions.stem: In a hover, in a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above, the pilot raises the collective to climb. To hold heading the pilot must:
options: Add right pedal as the nose swings left
Hold the pedals still; torque is unchanged
Add left pedal as the nose swings right
Move the cyclic left to stop the yaw
questions.explain: More collective means more engine power and more torque, which yaws the fuselage opposite to rotor rotation, to the right. Left pedal increases tail-rotor thrust to cancel it.

questions.stem: On a piston helicopter, the correlator is a mechanical linkage that:
options: Matches tail-rotor pitch to cyclic input
Keeps two rotors turning in step
Limits how far the cyclic can travel
Adjusts throttle as the collective moves
questions.explain: The correlator links collective and throttle so that raising collective opens the throttle and lowering it closes the throttle, helping hold RPM. A governor, if fitted, makes the fine corrections.

questions.stem: A helipad is at a pressure altitude of 4,000 feet and the outside air temperature is 25°C. Allowing about 120 feet per degree of deviation from standard temperature, the density altitude is closest to:
options: 7,000 feet
4,000 feet
1,800 feet
6,200 feet
questions.explain: Standard temperature at 4,000 feet is about 7°C (15°C minus 2°C per 1,000 feet). The air is 18°C warmer than standard, so density altitude is about 4,000 + (18 × 120) ≈ 6,200 feet. Using the full 25°C instead of the deviation gives the wrong 7,000 feet.

questions.stem: Which change, with everything else held constant, lowers density altitude and improves helicopter performance?
options: A rise in station pressure
A rise in relative humidity
A rise in air temperature
A rise in field elevation
questions.explain: Higher station pressure means denser air and a lower density altitude. Warmer air, higher elevation and moister air all reduce density; water vapor is lighter than the dry air it displaces, so humid air is less dense.

questions.stem: A helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above accelerates through ETL, and the tail rotor also becomes more efficient. This tends to yaw the nose:
options: Right, needing some left pedal
Right, needing some right pedal
Left, needing some left pedal
Left, needing some right pedal
questions.explain: In cleaner air the tail rotor produces more anti-torque thrust for the same pedal setting (translational thrust). That extra thrust swings the nose left, so the pilot eases in right pedal.

questions.stem: To counter translating tendency, many U.S. helicopters have the mast or cyclic rigging tilted slightly left. As a result, the helicopter usually hovers:
options: Right skid slightly low
Left skid slightly low
Nose slightly high
Level on both skids
questions.explain: The rotor disc is tilted left to cancel the tail rotor's push to the right, so the fuselage hangs with the left skid slightly low in a hover.

questions.stem: In a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above, an uncommanded right yaw begins at low airspeed, typical of LTE. The recommended response is:
options: Full right pedal and more collective for lift
Aft cyclic to slow down and raise collective
Neutral pedals while adding engine power
Full left pedal and forward cyclic for speed
questions.explain: Full left pedal and forward cyclic to gain airspeed are the immediate actions, and reducing collective, if altitude permits, cuts torque. Adding power increases torque and speeds up the right yaw.

questions.stem: For a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above, which maneuver carries the highest risk of loss of tail-rotor effectiveness?
options: A fast left turn into the wind
A slow left turn into the wind
A slow right turn with a tailwind
A fast right turn into the wind
questions.explain: LTE develops at low airspeed (below about 30 knots) with high power and certain wind directions. A slow downwind right turn is the classic case: the tailwind upsets tail-rotor thrust and weathervanes the tail, while the turn adds to the yaw already pushing the nose right.

questions.stem: A helicopter's empty weight is 1,500 lb at an arm of 100.0 in. A 200-lb pilot sits at 65.0 in and 120 lb of fuel is at 105.0 in. The loaded CG is closest to:
options: 96.5 inches
90.0 inches
95.9 inches
100.0 inches
questions.explain: Moments: 150,000 + 13,000 + 12,600 = 175,600 lb-in. Total weight: 1,820 lb. CG = 175,600 ÷ 1,820 ≈ 96.5 in. Leaving out the fuel gives 95.9 in, and averaging the three arms gives 90.0 in.

questions.stem: A helicopter's fuel tank sits aft of its loaded center of gravity. As fuel burns off during the flight, the CG will:
options: Move forward, away from the tank
Move aft, toward the fuel tank
Stay fixed, since the datum is fixed
Move aft and then return forward
questions.explain: Removing weight from a point behind the CG shifts the CG forward, away from where the weight was lost. This is why pilots check that both takeoff and landing CG fall within limits.

questions.stem: A METAR reports the sky condition as FEW005 SCT012 BKN025 OVC040. The ceiling is:
options: 1,200 feet AGL
2,500 feet AGL
500 feet AGL
4,000 feet AGL
questions.explain: A ceiling is the lowest layer reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC), or a vertical visibility. FEW and SCT layers do not count, so the ceiling is the broken layer at 2,500 feet AGL.

questions.stem: On approach, an aircraft flies straight through a microburst. In order, the crew will typically meet:
options: A tailwind, then a downdraft, then a headwind
A downdraft, then a headwind, then an updraft
A headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind
A crosswind, then an updraft, then a tailwind
questions.explain: The outflow first gives a headwind that raises airspeed and performance, then a strong downdraft in the core, then a tailwind that sharply cuts airspeed. The tailwind phase close to the ground is the most dangerous.

questions.stem: Surface temperature is 20°C and dewpoint is 12°C. Using the usual temperature-dewpoint convergence rate, the base of cumulus clouds is about:
options: 3,200 feet AGL
4,000 feet AGL
8,000 feet AGL
1,600 feet AGL
questions.explain: Temperature and dewpoint converge at about 2.5°C (4.4°F) per 1,000 feet. An 8°C spread ÷ 2.5 = 3.2, so cloud base is near 3,200 feet AGL. Using the 2°C standard lapse rate instead gives the wrong 4,000 feet.

questions.stem: Freezing rain reported at the surface tells a pilot that:
options: Warmer, above-freezing air lies aloft
Clear ice forms only at high altitude
The air is below freezing at all levels
Rain is evaporating before it lands
questions.explain: Freezing rain falls as rain from a warm layer aloft into below-freezing air near the surface, where it freezes on contact. Flight below the warm layer means clear ice; if the air were below freezing at all levels, the precipitation would fall as snow.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions is typical of a stable air mass?
options: Cumuliform cloud, rough air, good visibility
Stratiform cloud, rough air, good visibility
Cumuliform cloud, smooth air, poor visibility
Stratiform cloud, smooth air, poor visibility
questions.explain: Stable air resists vertical motion, so clouds spread in layers, the air is smooth and haze or smoke stays trapped near the surface, cutting visibility. Unstable air gives cumuliform cloud, turbulence and good visibility outside showers.

questions.stem: Below 10,000 feet MSL in Class D airspace, basic VFR requires 3 statute miles visibility and a cloud clearance of:
options: 1,000 ft below, 500 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
Clear of clouds, with no set distances
500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
questions.explain: Classes C, D and E below 10,000 feet MSL use 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontal. Clear of clouds is the Class B rule, and 1,000 / 1,000 / 1 statute mile applies in Class E at or above 10,000 feet MSL.

questions.stem: Under 14 CFR Part 91, Special VFR rules treat helicopters differently from airplanes because helicopters:
options: Need 3 miles visibility rather than 1
Must stay 500 feet below the clouds
May never fly Special VFR at night
Have no 1-mile visibility minimum
questions.explain: Section 91.157 requires 1 statute mile visibility for Special VFR in aircraft other than helicopters. Helicopters must still remain clear of clouds, and they are also exempt from the night instrument-rating and equipment requirement that applies to other aircraft.

questions.stem: Before a VFR helicopter enters Class C airspace, the pilot must:
options: Receive the words "cleared into" from ATC
File a VFR flight plan with flight service
Establish two-way radio contact with ATC
Hold an instrument rating and clearance
questions.explain: Class C requires two-way radio communication before entry, which is established when ATC answers using the aircraft's call sign. An explicit "cleared into" clearance is the Class B requirement.

questions.stem: A helicopter and a glider are converging at about the same altitude, with the helicopter on the glider's right. Which aircraft has the right-of-way?
options: The helicopter, since it is on the right
The glider, whatever its position
The helicopter, as the faster aircraft
The aircraft at the lower altitude
questions.explain: The aircraft-on-the-right rule applies only between aircraft of the same category. Between categories, a glider has right-of-way over airships, airplanes and rotorcraft; only balloons and aircraft in distress rank above it.

questions.stem: Under 14 CFR 91.151, a helicopter on a VFR flight must carry enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly, at normal cruising speed, for at least:
options: 30 minutes
20 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
questions.explain: Rotorcraft need a 20-minute VFR reserve. Airplanes need 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night, which are the common wrong answers.

questions.stem: A helicopter flies from an area of high pressure into an area of lower pressure without resetting the altimeter. Its true altitude will be:
options: Higher than indicated
Equal to the indicated altitude
Higher, then lower than indicated
Lower than indicated
questions.explain: With the old, higher setting still in the window, the altimeter over-reads in the low-pressure area, so the aircraft is lower than indicated: high to low, look out below. The error moves the aircraft toward terrain.

questions.stem: An aircraft in flight receives a flashing red light-gun signal from the control tower. This means:
options: Give way to other aircraft and keep circling
Return for landing and await a steady green
The airport is unsafe; do not land
Exercise extreme caution in the pattern
questions.explain: In flight, flashing red means the airport is unsafe and the aircraft must not land. Steady red means give way and continue circling, flashing green means return for landing, and alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution.

questions.stem: A helicopter in VFR flight loses all two-way radio communication. Which transponder code should the pilot set?
questions.explain: 7600 signals lost communications. 7500 is unlawful interference (hijack), 7700 is a general emergency, and 1200 is the standard VFR code.

questions.stem: Ice completely blocks the static port while the pitot tube stays clear. Which instruments will give unreliable readings?
options: The altimeter and the VSI only
The airspeed indicator alone
The attitude and heading gyros
The altimeter, VSI and airspeed
questions.explain: The altimeter and VSI work only from static pressure, and the airspeed indicator compares pitot pressure with static pressure, so all three are affected. The gyroscopic attitude and heading indicators do not use the pitot-static system.

questions.stem: Both the pitot tube's ram-air inlet and its drain hole become blocked, but the static port is clear. As the aircraft climbs, the airspeed indicator will:
options: Drop to zero and stay there
Freeze at the last reading
Show increasing airspeed
Show decreasing airspeed
questions.explain: Pressure trapped in the pitot line stays constant while static pressure falls in the climb, so the difference grows and the indicator reads higher, acting like an altimeter. If only the ram inlet blocks and the drain hole stays open, the reading falls to zero.

questions.stem: Flying on an easterly heading in the Northern Hemisphere, the pilot accelerates. The magnetic compass will briefly indicate:
options: A turn toward the south
No change in heading
A turn toward the north
A turn toward the west
questions.explain: Acceleration error follows ANDS: accelerate north, decelerate south. On east or west headings, speeding up swings the compass toward north and slowing down swings it toward south, though the heading has not changed.

questions.stem: Pilots realign the heading indicator with the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes because of:
options: Gyroscopic rigidity
Gyroscopic precession
Magnetic dip and turning error
Compass deviation error
questions.explain: Friction in the gyro makes it precess and drift away from the correct heading over time. Rigidity in space is what makes the gyro useful in the first place; dip and deviation are magnetic compass errors.

questions.stem: In the U.S. military designation HH-60M, the first "H" identifies the aircraft's:
options: Heavy-lift cargo mission
Helicopter vehicle type
Search-and-rescue mission
Hover-training mission
questions.explain: The letter before the type letter is the modified mission; H means search and rescue or medical evacuation. The second H is the basic vehicle type (helicopter), and M is the series. The Army's HH-60M is its MEDEVAC Black Hawk.

questions.stem: Which Army terrain-flight mode uses varying airspeed and varying altitude, flown as close to the earth's surface as vegetation and obstacles permit?
options: Low-level flight
Contour flight
Nap-of-the-earth flight
Terrain-following flight
questions.explain: NOE flight varies both airspeed and altitude to use terrain and vegetation for concealment. Contour flight follows the terrain at a generally constant airspeed with varying altitude, and low-level flight holds a constant airspeed and altitude.

questions.stem: Landing on fine, dry dust, a crew wants to keep outside visual references as long as possible. Which technique best reduces brownout risk?
options: Stop at a high hover to let the dust settle
Land with no hover, staying ahead of the dust
Descend slowly and vertically from a high hover
Hold a low hover with extra power before landing
questions.explain: Brownout comes from rotor downwash lifting dust that engulfs the aircraft. Keeping forward movement to touchdown leaves the dust cloud behind the crew; hovering, especially low or descending slowly, lets the cloud build around the aircraft.

questions.stem: During a rapid acceleration on a dark night takeoff with no visible horizon, a pilot may falsely feel that the aircraft is:
options: Pitching nose-up, and push the nose down
Pitching nose-down, and pull the nose up
Banking left, and roll back to the right
Yawing right, and add opposite left pedal
questions.explain: This is the somatogravic illusion: forward acceleration presses the otolith organs the same way a nose-up tilt would. A pilot who trusts the feeling may push the nose down toward the ground. Deceleration gives the opposite, nose-down sensation.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide from a leaking cabin heater stops the blood from carrying enough oxygen. This is classed as:
options: Hypoxic hypoxia
Hypemic hypoxia
Stagnant hypoxia
Histotoxic hypoxia
questions.explain: Hypemic hypoxia is a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, as when carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin. Hypoxic hypoxia comes from low oxygen pressure at altitude, stagnant from poor circulation, and histotoxic from cells unable to use oxygen, for example after alcohol.

questions.stem: In cruise, a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above suffers a complete tail-rotor drive failure. The expected yaw and corrective action are:
options: Nose left; raise collective and climb
Nose right; add power and full left pedal
Nose right; lower collective and autorotate
Nose left; lower collective and autorotate
questions.explain: With no tail-rotor thrust, main-rotor torque swings the nose right. Lowering collective and entering autorotation removes engine torque, while forward airspeed and the vertical fin help with directional control. Adding power only increases the yaw, and pedals do nothing once the drive has failed.

questions.stem: In a level, coordinated 60-degree banked turn, the load factor and the stall speed, compared with straight-and-level flight, are about:
options: 1.5 G; stall speed 22% higher
3 G; stall speed 73% higher
2 G; stall speed 100% higher
2 G; stall speed 41% higher
questions.explain: Load factor in a level turn is 1 ÷ cos(bank) = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 G. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor: √2 ≈ 1.41, so about 41 percent higher. In a helicopter the same loading raises blade angle of attack and brings retreating blade stall closer.

questions.stem: An airplane pilot rolls right using ailerons alone. The nose briefly yaws left because:
options: The left wing's lowered aileron adds drag
The right wing's raised aileron adds drag
Propeller torque pushes the nose to the left
The rudder trails to the left during the roll
questions.explain: Rolling right lowers the left aileron, which raises lift and induced drag on the rising left wing and drags the nose left (adverse yaw). Coordinated right rudder counters it.

questions.stem: Compared with the airspeed for minimum rate of descent in autorotation, the airspeed for maximum glide distance is:
options: Lower, to stretch the time aloft
Identical, since both use best L/D
Near zero, for a vertical descent
Higher, trading sink rate for range
questions.explain: Minimum-descent airspeed keeps the helicopter aloft longest. Flying faster, at max-glide airspeed, raises the rate of descent but covers more ground for each foot lost. A vertical autorotation gives a high descent rate and no forward distance.

questions.stem: During the flare at the bottom of an autorotation, the pilot applies aft cyclic. The effect on rotor RPM is that it:
options: Drops, as the disc tilts out of the airflow
Stays fixed, because the governor holds it
Rises, as more air flows up through the disc
Falls toward zero as lift is traded for speed
questions.explain: Tilting the disc aft increases the upward airflow through it, so rotor RPM rises while airspeed and descent rate fall. The engine is disengaged, so no governor is holding rotor RPM.

questions.stem: On a typical helicopter power-required curve, the least power is needed to hold altitude:
options: In a hover out of ground effect
In a hover in ground effect
At a moderate forward airspeed
At the never-exceed speed
questions.explain: In a hover the rotor must create all its own inflow, so induced power is high. As airspeed builds, translational lift sharply reduces induced power while parasite power grows slowly at first. The low point of the curve, at a moderate airspeed, is the best-endurance and best rate-of-climb speed.

questions.stem: In a free-turbine turboshaft engine, such as those on the UH-60, the power turbine (N2 or Np) drives:
options: The rotors through the transmission
The compressor that feeds the combustor
Only the starter-generator and fuel pump
The exhaust nozzle to produce jet thrust
questions.explain: The gas producer turbine (N1 or Ng) drives the compressor. The separate free power turbine (N2 or Np) has no mechanical link to it and drives the output shaft to the transmission and rotors.

questions.stem: A true course of 090° is plotted in an area where magnetic variation is 10° east. The magnetic course is:
questions.explain: East is least, west is best: subtract easterly variation and add westerly. 090° minus 10° gives a magnetic course of 080°. Adding it (100°) is the common mistake.

questions.stem: In Army aviation operations, a FARP is a:
options: Forward arming and refueling point
Field aircraft repair point
Flight approach reference point
Forward aviation recovery position
questions.explain: A forward arming and refueling point is a temporary site set up close to the area of operations so aircraft can rearm and refuel quickly without returning to their main base.

questions.stem: Compared with unaided daytime vision, a key limitation of aviator night vision goggles (ANVIS) is that:
options: They need at least a half moon to work
Their field of view is only about 40°
They cannot be used near any city lights
Their image lags a few seconds behind
questions.explain: ANVIS gives roughly a 40-degree field of view, far narrower than unaided vision, so crews must scan continuously by moving their heads. The goggles amplify starlight as well as moonlight and work near cultural lighting, though bright lights cause halos.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Swans are the heaviest birds capable of powered flight.
Migrating birds navigate across oceans using the stars.
Bird flight relies on physical principles like lift and drag.
Feathers keep birds warm as well as helping them fly.
questions.passage:
Watch a gull hang almost motionless above a harbor and it is easy to assume that flight is effortless. In truth, every soaring bird is solving a constant physical problem: how to stay aloft without falling and how to move forward without stalling. The secret lies mostly in the shape of the wing. A bird's wing is curved on top and flatter underneath, a form called an airfoil. As the wing slices through the air, the flow moving over the curved upper surface travels faster than the flow beneath it. This difference in speed lowers the pressure above the wing, and the higher pressure below pushes the wing upward. That upward push is what pilots and biologists alike call lift.

Lift alone is not enough. A bird must also overcome drag, the resistance created as its body pushes air aside. Larger, heavier birds such as swans need powerful chest muscles and rapid wingbeats to generate the thrust that carries them forward. Smaller birds spend less energy per beat but must flap far more often. Soaring species, by contrast, have learned to let the atmosphere do much of the work. They ride columns of warm rising air, called thermals, spiraling upward without a single flap, then glide slowly downward to the next thermal.

Feathers make these feats possible. The long, stiff feathers at the wingtip can be spread like fingers to reduce the swirling turbulence that would otherwise drag a bird backward. When a bird needs to slow down to land, it tilts its wings sharply, trading smooth airflow for a burst of braking resistance. Understanding these principles did not merely satisfy curiosity; it gave early aircraft designers a working model. Nature, it turned out, had been refining the airfoil for millions of years before any engineer sketched a wing.
questions.explain: The passage explains lift, drag, and how these principles gave aircraft designers a working model. The other options state real-world facts the text never makes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what lowers the air pressure above a bird's wing?
options: Air flows faster over the curved upper surface.
The wingtip feathers spread apart like fingers.
The bird beats its wings rapidly and steadily.
Warm rising thermals push upward on the wing.

options: have far weaker chest muscles than any swan.

do not need to overcome any drag while in the air.

options: the braking resistance a bird uses to land.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: Nightingale came from a wealthy and disapproving family.
Soldiers admired Nightingale for her nightly rounds with a lamp.
Hospitals in the 1850s were dangerously dirty and crowded.
Nightingale's lasting legacy was using data to drive reform.
questions.passage:
When Florence Nightingale arrived at the military hospital in Scutari in 1854, she found conditions that shocked even hardened army officers. Wounded soldiers lay on bare floors in corridors slick with filth. Rats moved freely among the beds, and clean water was scarce. Far more men were dying from infections, fever, and dysentery than from the wounds that had brought them there. Nightingale, who had trained as a nurse against the wishes of her wealthy family, set about changing this not with dramatic gestures but with relentless organization.

She insisted on scrubbing floors, ventilating wards, and supplying proper food and laundry. She kept meticulous records of how many men entered the hospital and how many died, and of what causes. It was this habit of careful counting that would prove her most lasting contribution. Back in England, she used the figures to argue, with charts of her own design, that most deaths were preventable and rooted in poor sanitation rather than in battle. Officials who might have dismissed a passionate speech could not easily ignore columns of hard numbers.

Her nighttime rounds, lamp in hand, earned her the affectionate name the soldiers gave her, and the public imagined a gentle comforter. Yet the woman behind the legend was above all an analyst and a reformer. In later decades, often confined to her home by chronic illness, she advised governments on hospital design and public health, shaping institutions she would never visit. She lived long enough to see nursing transformed from a job for the desperate into a respected profession. Nightingale's true monument was not the lamp of sentiment but the quiet insistence that evidence, gathered patiently and presented clearly, could save lives on a scale no single bedside visit ever could.
questions.explain: The passage argues her most lasting contribution was careful record-keeping and statistics used to push sanitary reform; the others are supporting details.

starvation caused by a total lack of any food.
infections and diseases such as fever and dysentery.

questions.stem: Which statement best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The fifteen-minute city puts daily needs within a short walk.
Private cars have made modern cities far too noisy and dirty.
Poorer neighborhoods are always ignored by city planners.
Rezoning a city is slow, costly, and politically divisive.
questions.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners treated the private car as the organizing principle of urban life. Neighborhoods were spread out, shops were pushed into distant malls, and workplaces were clustered downtown, all connected by wide roads. The result was cities in which almost every errand required a drive. In recent years a competing idea has gained ground, often called the fifteen-minute city. Its premise is simple: the things people need most often, such as groceries, schools, clinics, parks, and work, should lie within a short walk or bicycle ride of home.

Supporters argue that such an arrangement brings several benefits at once. Residents spend less time commuting and more time with family or in their community. Local shops thrive because people pass them on foot rather than speeding by. Streets grow quieter and cleaner as car traffic falls, and the exercise built into daily errands improves public health. Cities also become more resilient, since a neighborhood that meets its own daily needs is less paralyzed when fuel prices spike or transit systems fail.

The idea is not without critics. Some worry that concentrating amenities in wealthier districts could leave poorer neighborhoods behind, deepening rather than closing the gap between them. Others note that reshaping a city built for cars is slow, expensive, and politically contentious, requiring years of patient rezoning. A handful of commentators have even spun conspiracy theories, imagining the plans as a scheme to confine citizens to their districts. Planners respond that the goal is precisely the opposite: to give people more freedom by making a car optional rather than mandatory. Whether or not the label endures, the underlying question is likely to shape urban design for a generation, namely how to build places that serve the people who live in them rather than the machines they drive.
questions.explain: The passage introduces and evaluates the fifteen-minute city concept; the other options are single benefits or criticisms, not the main idea.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Renaissance inventors built the first working helicopters.
The helicopter's central challenge was achieving control.
Helicopters are far more useful than any fixed-wing plane.
Toy rotors carved from wood first inspired real aircraft.
questions.passage:
The dream of rising straight up into the air is older than the airplane. Sketches of screw-like flying machines appear in notebooks from the Renaissance, and children in Europe and Asia had long played with spinning toy rotors carved from wood. Turning that dream into a machine that could carry a person, however, took centuries, and it defeated many capable inventors. The problem was not simply getting a rotor to lift a craft off the ground. The deeper difficulty was control.

A fixed-wing airplane, once moving forward, is reasonably stable. A helicopter hovering in place is not. As the main rotor spins one way, it tries to spin the fuselage the opposite way, threatening to send the whole craft into a hopeless twirl. Early experimenters tried mounting two rotors turning in opposite directions to cancel this effect. The breakthrough that made the modern helicopter practical came when designers added a small vertical rotor on the tail. By pushing sideways, the tail rotor counteracts the twisting force and, when adjusted, lets the pilot swing the nose left or right at will.

Just as important was a mechanism allowing the pitch of each blade to change as it rotates, so that lift could be tilted in any direction. With it, a pilot could move forward, backward, or sideways, or hold a steady hover. Once these controls were mastered, the helicopter found work that no airplane could match. It could lift a stranded climber from a cliff, drop supplies where no runway existed, or lower a rescuer onto a sinking ship. What had begun as a whimsical toy and a Renaissance daydream became, within a single lifetime, one of the most versatile machines ever built, valued less for its speed than for its stubborn refusal to need a runway at all.
questions.explain: The passage stresses that control, not merely lift, was the deep difficulty, solved by the tail rotor and variable blade pitch.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Bad weather was the greatest threat the airlift crews had to overcome.
The Soviet Union ended the blockade because the airlift embarrassed it.
Tempelhof airfield was too small to handle the volume of the airlift.
The airlift succeeded mainly through strict, repeatable procedures.
questions.passage:
When Soviet forces cut the road, rail and canal routes into West Berlin in June 1948, few officials believed the city's two million residents could be supplied by air. Early flights were improvised: crews flew whenever an aircraft was ready, and on one stormy day in August so many aircraft stacked up over Tempelhof airfield that those still circling were ordered back to their bases.

That failure convinced Major General William Tunner that the airlift's real enemy was not the weather but irregularity. He imposed a rigid rhythm. Aircraft took off at fixed intervals, flew assigned altitudes along narrow corridors, and were allowed only one attempt at landing. A pilot who missed his approach did not circle for another try; he flew home with his cargo, and the next aircraft landed in his place. Crews were told to stay with their aircraft during unloading, so that a turnaround took minutes rather than hours.

The results surprised even the planners. By the spring of 1949 the airlift was delivering more cargo than had reached the city by rail before the blockade, and in May the Soviet Union lifted the restrictions. Historians still debate whether the blockade ended because the airlift worked or because Moscow judged the political cost too high. What is clear is that a problem of supply had been solved less by heroics than by discipline.
questions.explain: The passage credits Tunner's rigid system, not heroics, for the airlift's success. It says weather was not the real enemy, and it leaves the reason the blockade ended open to debate.

He diverted to another Berlin airfield to land there.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Pilot error caused most airliner accidents in thunderstorms during the 1970s.
Doppler radar was invented in order to study the downdrafts behind crashes.
Fujita's microburst theory, first doubted, was later confirmed by measurement.
Airline training in the 1980s largely ignored the danger of thunderstorms.
questions.passage:
In June 1975 an airliner crashed short of the runway at New York's Kennedy Airport during a thunderstorm. Investigators first suspected pilot error, but the meteorologist Tetsuya Theodore Fujita, studying the flight records, proposed something few colleagues accepted: a small, intense column of sinking air that struck the ground and spread outward in all directions. He called it a downburst, and later used the term microburst for the smallest and most violent kind.

Many atmospheric scientists were unconvinced. Downdrafts were well known, but most experts doubted that one could be strong and concentrated enough to force a heavy jet toward the ground. Fujita's evidence, critics noted, came largely from reconstructing damage patterns and flight data after the fact rather than from direct measurement.

The debate was settled by instruments. In 1982 a field project near Denver used Doppler radar to observe dozens of microbursts, many lasting only a few minutes and spanning less than two and a half miles. The data matched Fujita's description closely. Airlines and regulators responded with new training that taught crews to recognize the sudden gain in airspeed that often comes just before the dangerous downdraft and tailwind, and airports later installed radar designed to detect wind shear along approach paths.
questions.explain: The passage traces Fujita's idea from skepticism to confirmation by Doppler radar and the safety changes that followed. The other choices misstate or go beyond the text.

In June 1975 an airliner crashed short of the runway at New York's Kennedy Airport during a thunderstorm. Investigators first suspected pilot error, but the meteorologist Tetsuya Theodore Fujita, studying the flight records, proposed something few colleagues accepted: a small, intense column of sinking air that struck the ground and spread outward in all directions. He called it a downburst, and later used the term microburst for the smallest and most violent kind.

Many atmospheric scientists were unconvinced. Downdrafts were well known, but most experts doubted that one could be strong and concentrated enough to force a heavy jet toward the ground. Fujita's evidence, critics noted, came largely from reconstructing damage patterns and flight data after the fact rather than from direct measurement.

The debate was settled by instruments. In 1982 a field project near Denver used Doppler radar to observe dozens of microbursts, many lasting only a few minutes and spanning less than two and a half miles. The data matched Fujita's description closely. Airlines and regulators responded with new training that taught crews to recognize the sudden gain in airspeed that often comes just before the dangerous downdraft and tailwind, and airports later installed radar designed to detect wind shear along approach paths.
questions.explain: "The debate was settled by instruments" means the disagreement was resolved by measurement. The other meanings of "settle" do not fit a debate.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The raid failed because the bombers were launched too far from Japan.

The raid led directly and unavoidably to Japan's defeat in the war.
The raid did little damage but had major effects on morale and strategy.
questions.passage:
On the morning of 18 April 1942, sixteen Army B-25 bombers lumbered off the deck of the aircraft carrier Hornet, a feat never before attempted in combat. The plan, led by Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle, called for the bombers to strike targets in Japan and fly on to airfields in China, since the aircraft were too large to land back aboard the carrier. When a Japanese patrol boat spotted the task force hours before the planned launch, the commanders faced a hard choice: abandon the mission or launch early, well beyond the range the crews had planned for. They launched.

The bombs did little physical damage. None of the aircraft reached its intended airfield; most crews bailed out or crash-landed in China, and one crew landed in the Soviet Union, where it was interned. Judged purely as a bombing raid, the operation was a failure.

Yet military historians rarely judge it that way. The raid lifted American morale at a time when the war news had been almost uniformly bad, and it shocked Japanese leaders who had assumed the home islands were beyond reach. Some historians argue that the embarrassment strengthened Japan's resolve to push its defensive perimeter outward, a decision that helped lead to the Battle of Midway, where Japan lost four fleet carriers. The raid's greatest effects, in other words, were felt far from its targets.
questions.explain: The passage contrasts the raid's slight physical damage with its effects on American morale and Japanese strategy. It says the bombers could not land on the carrier and never claims the raid decided the war.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Pilots must trust instruments because the inner ear can misread long turns.
Experienced pilots no longer feel the false sensations that trouble students.

Pilots should avoid any turn that lasts longer than about twenty seconds.
questions.passage:
The inner ear contains three fluid-filled semicircular canals, set roughly at right angles to one another, that let the brain sense rotation. When the head turns, the fluid lags behind the canal walls and bends tiny hair cells, signaling motion. The system works well for the brief turns of everyday life. In flight it can be dangerously misleading.

The problem is that the canals detect changes in rotation, not rotation itself. If a pilot enters a gradual turn and holds it, the fluid soon catches up with the canal walls and the hair cells straighten. Within perhaps twenty seconds the brain concludes that the turn has stopped, although the aircraft is still banked. If the pilot then rolls level, the fluid moves again, and the brain reports a turn in the opposite direction. A pilot without a visible horizon may lean, or even roll back into the original bank, to make the false sensation go away.

Training cannot switch these sensations off. Experienced pilots feel them as strongly as students do. What training provides is a habit: when the body and the instruments disagree, believe the instruments. That habit is easy to state and surprisingly hard to keep, because the false sensation feels completely real at the moment it matters most.
questions.explain: The passage explains how the canals misread sustained turns and concludes that pilots must rely on instruments. It says experienced pilots still feel the illusions and never advises avoiding long turns.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Esperanto failed because scientists refused to learn an invented language.
Japan's balloon bombs were among the most effective weapons of the war.
B-29 crews were the first people ever to measure the jet stream's speed.
Ooishi found the jet stream, but his work had little early influence abroad.
questions.passage:
In the 1920s a Japanese meteorologist named Wasaburo Ooishi released hundreds of small balloons near Mount Fuji and tracked them by theodolite as they rose. His records revealed a band of remarkably fast westerly winds high above Japan, strongest in winter. Ooishi published his findings, but he wrote his reports in Esperanto, an invented language he hoped would become an international standard. Few meteorologists outside Japan read them.

The winds were, in effect, rediscovered by others. In 1944 American B-29 crews flying at high altitude over Japan met headwinds and tailwinds so strong that bombing accuracy suffered badly. Meanwhile, Japanese military planners who did know of Ooishi's work used it for a very different purpose. They launched thousands of paper and rubberized-silk balloons carrying small bombs, counting on the winter winds to carry them across the Pacific to North America within a few days. Most were lost at sea, and the campaign did little damage.

Today the jet stream is common knowledge; airlines plan eastbound routes to ride it and westbound routes to avoid it. Ooishi's story is sometimes told as a lesson about science and language. A discovery, it suggests, does not fully enter science when it is made, but when it is read.
questions.explain: The passage centers on Ooishi's discovery, why few outside Japan read it, and how the winds were later rediscovered. The balloon campaign is said to have done little damage.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The Bell H-13 was too fragile to be of much real use in Korea.
Helicopter evacuation showed that speed to surgery improves survival.
Evacuation crews in Vietnam suffered the heaviest losses of any unit.
Commanders took greater risks because the wounded could be flown out.
questions.passage:
During the Korean War, the U.S. Army's small Bell H-13 helicopters carried wounded soldiers in pods strapped to the outside of the aircraft. The machines were fragile, struggled in poor weather, and had no room for a medic to treat patients in flight. Yet they could reach a casualty in mountainous terrain within minutes and fly him directly to a surgical hospital, bypassing a journey by stretcher and truck that might take hours.

Army doctors noticed that the speed of evacuation mattered as much as the treatment that followed. A wounded soldier who reached surgery quickly was far more likely to survive than one whose care was delayed, even when both received the same operation. The lesson shaped planning for the next war. In Vietnam, the larger UH-1 Huey carried medics on board, so care began in the aircraft rather than at the hospital door. Crews often flew into areas still under fire, and many were killed or wounded doing so.

One might ask whether rapid evacuation encouraged commanders to accept riskier operations, knowing the wounded could be removed quickly. Whatever the answer, few military doctors would choose to return to the stretcher and the truck.
questions.explain: The passage centers on the lesson that rapid evacuation saves lives and how it shaped later practice. It raises the question of commanders' risk-taking without answering it.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Supercooled droplets freeze on aircraft and harm lift and drag.
Clear ice is more dangerous than rime ice because it is heavier.
Helicopters cannot fly safely through any kind of cloud.
Cloud water always freezes once the air drops below 0°C.
questions.passage:
Water does not always freeze at 0°C. In clouds, tiny droplets can remain liquid at temperatures well below freezing, sometimes colder than -20°C, because they lack a particle of dust or ice around which a crystal can begin to grow. Such droplets are called supercooled, and they stay liquid only as long as nothing disturbs them.

An aircraft is a very large disturbance. When it flies through a cloud of supercooled droplets, the droplets strike the leading edges of the wings, the windscreen and, on a helicopter, the rotor blades, and they freeze almost at once. Small droplets tend to freeze the instant they hit, trapping air and forming rough, milky rime ice. Larger droplets freeze more slowly; they spread back across the surface before hardening into clear ice, which is heavier, harder to see and harder to remove.

Ice harms flight less through its weight than through its shape. Even a thin, rough layer on a wing or rotor blade disrupts the smooth flow of air over the airfoil, cutting lift and adding drag. For a helicopter the problem is especially serious, because its rotor blades are its wings, and ice on them raises the power needed simply to stay in the air. Many helicopters are not certified to fly into known icing conditions at all.
questions.explain: The passage explains what supercooled droplets are, how they turn to ice on an aircraft, and why that ice degrades performance. It says ice harms mainly through shape, not weight.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The Tuskegee Airmen never lost a single bomber that they escorted.
Historians have shown that the airmen's reputation was exaggerated.
Mission records corrected a myth but confirmed the airmen's strong record.
The military ended segregation because of the airmen's combat record.
questions.passage:
For decades after the Second World War, it was widely repeated that the Tuskegee Airmen, the first Black military pilots in the U.S. Army Air Forces, had never lost a bomber they were escorting to enemy fighters. The claim appeared in newspapers, speeches and even official tributes. It was a powerful symbol, because these pilots had been trained and sent to war by a segregated military whose leaders often doubted they could fly in combat at all.

In the 2000s, a historian working with Air Force mission records examined the claim in detail. He found that a small number of bombers under the group's escort had in fact been shot down by enemy aircraft. Some admirers saw the finding as an attack on the airmen's reputation.

The same records, however, told a more interesting story. The group had lost fewer bombers than the average for the other escort groups in the same air force, and its pilots had earned that record against the same enemy, in the same skies, while facing doubts their white counterparts never had to answer. A legend of perfection had been replaced by a documented record of excellence. The historian's conclusion was not that the airmen had been overrated, but that they did not need a myth.
questions.explain: The records disproved the "never lost a bomber" claim while showing a better-than-average record. The author explicitly says the airmen were not overrated.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Atomic clocks are too unreliable to use aboard satellites in orbit.
GPS accuracy depends on correcting satellite clocks for relativity.
Einstein's theory matters mainly for the study of distant stars.
GPS satellites move fast enough to make their clocks gain time.
questions.passage:
Each satellite in the Global Positioning System carries an atomic clock and continuously broadcasts the time and its own position. A receiver on the ground compares the signals from several satellites. Because radio waves travel at a known speed, the time each signal takes to arrive reveals how far away each satellite is, and from those distances the receiver works out its own position. The method is simple in principle and unforgiving in practice: an error of one millionth of a second in timing becomes an error of about 300 meters in distance.

That sensitivity brings an unexpected branch of physics into play. According to Einstein's theory of relativity, a clock moving at high speed runs slightly slow, while a clock farther from Earth's gravity runs slightly fast. For GPS satellites, the second effect is the larger one. Left uncorrected, the satellite clocks would gain about 38 millionths of a second each day compared with clocks on the ground, and position errors would build up by several kilometers daily.

Engineers do not wait for the errors to appear. Before launch, the satellite clocks are deliberately set to tick at a slightly slower rate, so that once in orbit they keep time with the ground. Relativity, often thought of as a theory about distant stars and extreme speeds, is quietly at work every time a phone finds its location.
questions.explain: The passage explains why timing must be precise and how relativity would throw the clocks off without a deliberate correction. It says the gain comes from weaker gravity, not speed.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The Army's 1907 specification was impossible for any aircraft to meet.

questions.passage:
In December 1907 the U.S. Army Signal Corps advertised for a flying machine. The specification seemed ambitious to the point of fantasy: the aircraft had to carry two people, fly at least 40 miles per hour, stay aloft for an hour, and be able to be taken apart for transport by Army wagon. Newspapers mocked the idea, and dozens of bidders who had never flown anything submitted offers anyway.

The Wright brothers took the specification seriously. In September 1908 Orville Wright began trials at Fort Myer, Virginia, and within days set endurance records that stunned observers. Then, on 17 September, a propeller cracked during a flight with Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge aboard as a passenger. The aircraft crashed. Orville was badly injured, and Selfridge died, becoming the first person killed in the crash of a powered airplane.

The Army did not cancel the program. The Wrights returned the following summer with a new machine, and in July 1909 it met every requirement. Because the contract paid a bonus for each mile per hour above 40, the brothers' speed of a little over 42 miles per hour earned them more than the base price. The aircraft became the Army's first airplane. Its purchase marked a quiet decision: the Army would now treat flight not as a curiosity but as a military tool worth its risks.
questions.explain: The passage follows the trials from the specification through the fatal crash to the Army's purchase and its decision to treat flight as a military tool.
